facts.text: In 1965 Gordon Moore, who held a PhD in chemistry, wrote an article for Electronics magazine predicting how quickly the number of components on integrated circuits would grow.
Moore’s 1965 plot showed that the number of components per chip had doubled each year since 1959, and he predicted the trend would continue for ten more years.
Moore later recalled that he expected chips to go from about 60 components to about 60,000 over those ten years.
Three years after the 1965 article, in 1968, Moore and Robert Noyce founded the company that became Intel.
Moore later revised his prediction: instead of doubling every year, the number of transistors on a chip would double about every two years.
Carver Mead, a computer scientist at Caltech, coined the name Moore’s law in the early 1970s; the name became widely used in the late 1970s.
Moore and his colleagues promoted his plot to encourage investment, and it served as a technology road map that guided the chip industry for about a quarter of a century.
An Intel scientist described Moore’s law as a relentless boss, because engineers must keep learning to make transistors smaller to stay on schedule.
In 2005 Moore described his law as a lucky guess that had received much more publicity than it deserved.
Transistors are the tiny switches that control the flow of electricity in a chip and make digital processing possible.
In the Our World in Data series, the leading microprocessor held about 2,300 transistors in 1971 (2,308 in the data) and 58.2 billion in 2021.
Derived from the dataset: 58.2 billion divided by 2,308 is about 25.2 million, so the 2021 count was roughly 25 million times the 1971 count.
Derived: doubling every two years for 50 years means 25 doublings, which multiplies a number by about 33.5 million, that is, by more than 33 million.
Derived from the dataset: the count grew about 58.8 times from 1971 to 1982, 22.9 times from 1982 to 1992, 71 times from 1992 to 2002, 11.8 times from 2002 to 2012, and 22.4 times from 2012 to 2021.
Derived: doubling every two years for the 9 years from 2012 to 2021 would multiply a number by about 22.6, close to the 22.4 times seen in the data.
As transistors shrank, the price per transistor and the price of computing fell sharply, which allowed computers to become smaller and more powerful without costing more.
The IBM 1401, a mainframe from the early 1960s, filled a room the size of a classroom and had the equivalent of only 16 kilobytes of memory.
Experts say Moore’s law may be reaching its limit: tens of billions of transistors now fit on a chip, and further shrinking saves much less power, so packing in more transistors creates heat.
An MIT researcher expects the predictability of Moore’s law to fade in the coming decade, with future gains coming from better software and from chip packaging, the ways chips are connected together.
